---
name: instruct-another-ai
description: Best practices for getting a step-function leap in performance from other AI agents when instructing or communicating with them. Note that Markdown docs are AI agents’ bread-and-butter, not only humans’. Load `instruct-another-ai` autonomously before spawning a sub-agent, creating a team of sub-agents, talking to a teammate agent, or writing documentation. Trigger words are “dispatch an agent”, “spawn a team”, etc.
---

## Why delegate at all?

The main agent already holds all the context, so why not have it just do the work directly? Context management. Both sub-agents and teams spin up a *fresh* context window and hand back only the bottom line, sparing you the token-heavy process that produced it. Two payoffs: (1) you reach the crux of the problem with plenty of headroom left in your own context window, instead of arriving running on fumes; and (2) you escape your own accrued bias.

The flip side: if none of these payoffs apply, don't delegate. The anti-pattern is the user asking for something straightforward and the main agent handing the *whole* task to another agent, ending the session: no context-window hygiene, no synergy, no parallelism, no bias mitigation, just duplicated tokens and a game of broken telephone.

Classic use cases — *generalize* the principles, this isn't a comprehensive list:
- **Exploration** — one sub-agent for a single domain, or parallel sub-agents when your can fan the scope out. Keeps your own context light, and parallel agents save wall-clock time too.
- **Debating the best plan** — an adversarial team handed the user's goal at large plus the exploration results. Synergistic judgement, and it mitigates any single teammate's bias.
- **Reviewing an implementation** — a sub-agent handed the user's goal at large, the exploration results, the finalized plan, and the implementation's commit SHA. Mitigates the main agent's bias toward its own work.

---

1. Orient the agent to the project: the user has mostly likely told you to load a context-gathering skill first thing in the session. Tell the AI agent to load the same skill, with the same arguments the user has specified. On top of that, if throughout the session, you have created, read or edited additional files that are not referenced by the skill, reference them too.  

2. Be generous in giving the agent wider context—understanding *why* it's performing the task will boost its performance. Don't micromanage or over-instruct it. The agent already has the same system prompt as you do out of the box (e.g. `CLAUDE.md` or `AGENTS.md`). It is essentially an equivalent instantiation of yourself. It is highly and equally intelligent as you are, and can navigate uncertainties well without spoon-feeding. What kind of input do YOU thrive on? Exactly — wide contextual understanding and aspired end state. Avoid prescribing instructions, giving "how-to" examples, providing examples as to what to think about, or dictating which files, symbols, or paths to look at; avoid any form of providing hints for possible answers for your own queries — this is circular and useless. Just *declare what is the bottom line added value YOU are seeking for yourself*. Instead of specifying which steps to take (dictating the "how" is bad), share with the agent only why it was dispatched and what you hope to gain. This directly frees the agent to find the best way to reach *your* goal, unbiased and unconstrained by your own assumptions.
    Essentially, all the “Don’ts” above over-fit the agent.
    <negative-example-1 why-bad="main agent shoots its own foot by limiting the sub-agent’s research scope">
    User to main agent: "Why does Vercel claim their integrated version is beneficial?"
    Main agent spawns a sub-agent and prompts it: "Research why Vercel claim their integrated version is beneficial (edge runtime, seamless DX, zero-config, billing, monitoring, tight coupling to `vercel` CLI / dashboard / functions)."
    </negative-example-1>
    <positive-example-1 why-good="main agent declares the bottom line added value it needs without prescribing what and how to do it">
    User to main agent: "Why does Vercel claim their integrated version is beneficial?"
    Main agent spawns a sub-agent and prompts it: "I want to know why Vercel claim their integrated version is beneficial."
    </positive-example-1>
    
    Example 2 settings: the `load-context` skill instructs to read CLAUDE.md, ARCHITECTURE.md, docs/webserver/API.md, docs/data/architecture.md, server/api.py, and server/db.py.    
    <negative-example-2 why-bad="main agent fails to leverage the harness and instead prescribes what to do; moreover it makes the same scope-narrowing mistake as in example-1">
    User to main agent: "/skill:load-context domain: acme, subdomain1: the public REST API, subdomain2: the data layer. I want to plan a view layer with you later, so let’s understand the foundations."
    Main agent spawns a sub-agent and prompts it: "Read CLAUDE.md, ARCHITECTURE.md, docs/webserver/API.md, docs/data/architecture.md, server/api.py, server/db.py, and summarize how the REST API and data layers work. Cover how function `server/api.py:from_db` fetches the data by calling the `server/db.py:get_data` function, and how [...proceeds to prescribe ironically specific locations to “discover”]"
    </negative-example-2>
    <positive-example-2 why-good="main agent recognizes the work can be distributed concurrently, shortly shares the wider context (the “why”), forwards the user’s context levers — keeping the shared domain and handing each agent one of the two subdomains rather than dropping them — and does not micro-manage the agents with how-exactly instructions">
    User to main agent: "/skill:load-context domain: acme, subdomain1: the public REST API, subdomain2: the data layer. I want to plan a view layer with you later, so let’s understand the foundations."
    Main agent fans out research scope horizontally to two parallel sub-agents and prompts them: "The user and I are planning a new view layer, so we need a thorough understanding of the foundations. [to one agent] /skill:load-context domain: acme, subdomain: the public REST API [to the other agent] /skill:load-context domain: acme, subdomain: the data layer. [to both] Study your subdomain deeply and exhaustively."
    [Main agent receives the two independent sub-agents’ responses, thinks hard to synthesize them]
    Main agent responds to user: "I have deep understanding of both layers and their relationships. What did you have in mind?"
    </positive-example-2>

    
    <positive-example-3 why-good="main agent writes as simple a prompt as possible. adds only what is necessary to get the reviewer up to speed. does not put words in the user’s mouth." note="this example has no negative counterpart. this is a positive example.">
    User to main agent: "Spawn a sub-agent to review your work. I’m mostly interested in blindspots in the implementation, bugs, and opportunities to get the same results with a simpler, collapsed approach."
    Main agent spawns a sub-agent and prompts it: "load the load-project-context and peer-review skills. the user asked me to <user request>. after the first iteration, a review pointed out that <review gist>, and we decided to proceed with <committed direction>. i’ve implemented it. review my work (the current main dirty tree). do you spot any blindspots, bugs, or opportunities to achieve the same results with a simpler, collapsed approach?"
    </positive-example-3>

3. Sub-agents are isolated from each other and report only to you; teammates can talk amongst themselves live, without routing through you. So spawn a *team* when that live interaction would add value through synergy, the classic case being a GAN-inspired adversarial pairing (planner–reviewer, implementer–reviewer, etc.) where one produces and the other pokes holes until both are content. Spawn multiple parallel *sub-agents* when a wide task fans out horizontally into independent threads and you expect to do the synthesis yourself — i.e. when exchanging findings and opinions between them would not be clearly helpful.

4. Since teammates talk to each other, tell each of them to load the this skill (`instruct-other-ai`) on top of the context-gathering skill. If you are spawning an adversary among them, tell it to load the `peer-review` skill too.

    Example 4 settings: at the session’s start the user ran `/skill:load-context domain: acme, subdomain1: the public REST API, subdomain2: the data layer`; the main session explored the code, and the user approved a plan to add rate limiting to the public REST API.
    <negative-example-4 why-bad="main agent burns its own context shuttling the diff and the feedback back and forth — dives into the sub-agent’s work and clogs its own context window worse than doing the task solo would have, acts as a reviewer when biased">
    User to main agent: "Great, go ahead and build it."
    Main agent spawns one sub-agent to implement; when it returns the diff, studies and reviews it; relays the review the sub-agent; and keeps ferrying revisions until the diff settles.
    </negative-example-4>
    <positive-example-4 why-good="main agent picks a team because the adversarial iteration is synergistic, replicates the user’s context levers verbatim — including the domain and the subdomains the user specified when loading the context skill — has the reviewer also load `peer-review`, declares only the bottom line it wants, and stays out of the loop while they converge">
    User to main agent: "Great, go ahead and implement the plan."
    Main agent spawns an implementer–reviewer team and prompts them: "/skill:load-context domain: acme, subdomain1: the public REST API, subdomain2: the data layer, then load `instruct-another-ai`. You are an implementer–reviewer team. Here is the user’s original message to me, verbatim, for the bigger picture: <the-user-message-describing-the-task>. [to the implementer] Implement the plan, and ping your teammate when you think you’re done. [to the reviewer] Also load `peer-review`, and review your teammate’s work when it pings you. [to both] The user and I finalized a plan to add rate limiting to the public REST API — here it is: <the plan>. Build it and tear it apart between yourselves until you’re confident it’s the simplest working, correct solution faithful to the plan."
    [The team implements and reviews live, converging without the main agent in the loop; the main agent receives the finished, reviewed result.]
    Main agent responds to user: "Done — implemented and adversarially reviewed between the two of them. Here’s what landed: …"
    </positive-example-4>

    **Note to Teammates:** Set your own status frequently. Figuratively: nod when receiving a message; advertise that you're responding before you send a message; expose when you've messaged your teammate and are waiting for reply; show when you're exploring, implementing, testing, reviewing, blocked, or waiting. Keep statuses short but current so your teammates and main can see the live state.

5. Subagents and teams can take a long time to run - use a 20-minute timeout.

6. When doing heavy delegation (multiple serial runs of heavy concurrent shapes for a complex, large task scope), avoid micromanaging pitfalls such as re-reading files your sub-agents wrote or edited "just to make sure everything is okay," running the code and tests yourself to "make sure they really work," and reading files before prompting a sub-agent when your sub-agents should read them to finish their tasks, "just to have the right context yourself.". Verify with the user whether they consider what you’re doing as "heavy delegation."

  1   # Eager `/agent` argument autocomplete plan
  2   
  3   > Status: in progress — policy locked; TDD characterization underway; no production implementation yet.  
  4   > Updated: 2026-07-16.  
  5   > This file is also the execution ledger; update the status table as work proceeds.
  6   
  7   ## Success means the editor and runtime cannot disagree
  8   
  9   The finished interaction is:
 10   
 11   1. The user types `/agent ` and then `-` at a cursor position where the command grammar permits another option.
 12   2. An autocomplete menu visibly opens immediately, without Tab and without relying on incidental Pi editor behavior.
 13   3. The menu contains every supported spelling not already semantically present, with labels such as `-m <model>` and `--thinking <level>`.
 14   4. Accepting a boolean option or an enumerable value leaves exactly one trailing space and advances the cursor after it.
 15   5. Accepting a free-form value option inserts an empty quoted slot plus a trailing separator—such as `--system-prompt "" `—and places the cursor between the quotes so typing is protected without escape anxiety.
 16   6. If the option has enumerable values, its value menu opens immediately after the option menu closes.
 17   7. If the option is path-valued, filesystem completion opens inside the guarded quotes and continues eagerly through directories.
 18   8. Once command parsing has entered task prose, option autocomplete never reappears.
 19   9. Submitted input and pre-submit editor input are interpreted by the same option declaration and state engine.
 20   
 21   The current ground truth is that typing `-` does **not** visibly open such a menu. Source-level evidence that Pi may request autocomplete in some slash contexts is not the product behavior and will not be treated as the trigger mechanism.
 22   
 23   Current baseline: 61 parser/forwarding tests in `tests/runner.test.ts` and four widget tests in `tests/widget.test.ts` are green. `tests/command-line.test.ts` contains the first intentional RED test: `-m` and `--model` must parse as one semantic option.

 40   # Pass 2 — Dependencies, forks, and delivery risk

 42   ## The graph has one policy gate and one critical implementation path

 47               ├──────────────┐
 48               ▼              ▼
 49   B. Characterize parser   C. Characterize editor integration
 50               └──────┬───────┘

 70   ## Policy decisions and approved branches
 71   
 72   ### A1. Free-form and secret values — approved: guarded quoted slot
 73   
 74   Some effective options accept arbitrary text rather than a finite candidate set, such as `--system-prompt` and `--append-system-prompt`.
 75   
 76   Selecting one inserts the option, one separator, an empty quoted value, and one trailing separator. The cursor lands inside the quotes:
 77   
 78   ```text
 79   /agent --system-prompt "│" 
 80   ```
 81   
 82   The cursor is intentionally not at the end. The user types directly into the protected literal; the closing quote and the command’s trailing separator are already present. This is an editable empty value, not a fake placeholder and not a second menu.
 83   
 84   ### A2. Recognized options that do not affect the SDK child — approved: effective only
 85   
 86   `resolveForwardedOptions()` currently applies model/thinking, tool, and resource-loader settings. Several other recognized Pi flags are parsed but have no child-session effect.
 87   
 88   Autocomplete suggests only options that actually affect the child. Runtime parsing continues recognizing the legacy set so this feature does not silently change existing submitted-command behavior.
 89   
 90   ### A3. Aliases in the menu — approved: every spelling, semantic suppression
 91   
 92   A single `-` prefix may match both short and long spellings, so both `-i` and `--isolate` appear as separate rows. Once the fragment becomes `--`, only long spellings remain. Selecting or manually typing either spelling marks the semantic option present and suppresses every alias thereafter.
 93   
 94   ### A4. Path-valued options — approved: eager quoted traversal
 95   
 96   Effective path-valued examples include `--extension`/`-e`, `--skill`, `--prompt-template`, and `--theme`. Their values identify a file or directory on disk.
 97   
 98   Selecting one creates the same guarded shape—such as `/agent --skill "│" `—then immediately opens Pi’s filesystem menu inside the quotes. Selecting a directory keeps the cursor inside the quoted value and eagerly reopens the filesystem menu for the next segment. The closing quote and the command’s single trailing separator remain outside the traversal cursor, so recursive path completion does not require an exception to the spacing rule. Selecting a file moves the cursor after that separator: `/agent --skill "src/file.ts" │`.
 99   
100   ### A5. Model options — approved: one CLI-backed semantic option
101   
102   `-m` and `--model` are aliases. Both project to Pi’s `--model` input and resolve once through `resolveCliModel()`; `--provider` scopes either spelling. Selecting or typing either alias suppresses both in completion.
103   
104   ### Locked decisions
105   
106   - A single `-` fragment may offer both short and long spellings; a `--` fragment offers only long spellings.
107   - An already present semantic option is hidden under every alias, even if the runtime happens to accept repetitions. Users can still type a repeated option manually.
108   - `/agent-isolated` begins completion analysis with isolation already satisfied, so it does not suggest `-i` or `--isolate`.
109   - A completion domain receives its live catalog unchanged; an empty catalog is Pi’s normal picker outcome, not command-language policy.
110   - Selecting a file leaves the cursor after the preserved outer separator; selecting a directory keeps it inside the quotes.
111   - Blocked options remain recognizable for runtime errors and prose warnings but never appear in completion.
112   - Unknown dash-prefixed tokens preserve today’s runtime rule: they commit the remainder to prose rather than becoming parser errors.

131   ## 1. Lock behavior and write characterization tests

160   ## 2. Replace option sets with one declarative specification and scanner
161   
162   ### Intended source of truth
163   
164   Add `command-line.ts` with one ordered option declaration. Each semantic option records:
165   
166   - accepted names and preferred completion spelling;
167   - extension-owned, forwarded, or blocked role;
168   - boolean or value arity;
169   - placeholder and optional value-completion domain;
170   - whether autocomplete may suggest it;
171   - concise user-facing description.

175   ### State model
176   
177   ```text
178   ARGUMENTS
179     recognized boolean ───────────────→ ARGUMENTS
180     recognized value option ──────────→ EXPECT_VALUE(option)
181     blocked option ───────────────────→ ERROR in strict runtime mode
182     unknown/escaped/quoted/prose word ─→ PROSE
183   
184   EXPECT_VALUE(option)
185     next value token ─────────────────→ ARGUMENTS
186     end of input ─────────────────────→ INCOMPLETE
187   
188   PROSE
189     every remaining token ────────────→ PROSE
190   ```
191   
192   `PROSE` is terminal. Cursor analysis may observe a partial option token before it is committed as prose; strict submission retains today’s exact-token behavior.

195   
196   > Scan leading command input once while carrying a tagged state. Resolve option tokens through the single specification, consume one value token when required, and permanently enter prose on the first non-option token. Preserve token source spans, quote metadata, and the original prose offset. When a cursor is supplied, report the grammar state immediately around its active token plus the exact fragment span that completion may replace. Project strict runtime output from the same scan, applying the existing errors, warnings, dequoting, and backslash rules.

  1   # `/agent` command-line parser — specification
  2   
  3   This is the authoritative spec for how `parseAgentCommand` turns the raw string a user
  4   types after `/agent` / `/agent-isolated` into structured options plus a prose task.
  5   It supersedes the current generic-passthrough parser in `runner.ts`.
  6   
  7   ## 1. What the parser produces
  8   
  9   ```ts
 10   type ParsedAgentCommand = {
 11     modelReference?: string;   // from the extension's -m
 12     isolate: boolean;          // -i / --isolate
 13     context: boolean;          // -c / --context
 14     forwardedArgs: string[];   // recognized pi option tokens (+values) in input order, e.g. ["--thinking","high"]
 15     task: string;              // the prose prompt (backslash escapes applied, quotes kept). Never empty.
 16     warnings: string[];        // advisory messages (see §5). May be empty.
 17   };
 18   ```
 19   
 20   `forwardedArgs` contains **only** known, non-blocked pi options — never the extension's own
 21   options, never unknown/third-party tokens. It is later mapped to child-session inputs by
 22   `resolveForwardedOptions` (unchanged in spirit, but the unknown-flag path is removed).
 23   
 24   ## 2. The state machine (one-way: args → prose)
 25   
 26   Read whitespace-delimited tokens from the front. Start in **args mode**.
 27   
 28   - In args mode, classify each token (§4). A recognized option is consumed (with its value if it
 29     takes one) and we stay in args mode.
 30   - The **first** token that is not a recognized option flips us to **prose mode**, permanently.
 31     There is no path back to args mode.
 32   - **Prose** is the remainder of the original input starting at the flip token, kept verbatim
 33     except for backslash-escape processing (§6). Whitespace and quotes are preserved exactly.
 34   
 35   If options are consumed and nothing is left, that is a usage error (a task is required).
 36   When the very first token is prose, the entire original input is the task, including any
 37   leading whitespace (unchanged from today).
 38   
 39   ## 3. Recognized options
 40   
 41   ### 3a. Extension options — consumed here, NOT forwarded to pi
 42   | Token(s) | Arity | Effect |
 43   |---|---|---|
 44   | `-m <value>` | value | `modelReference` |
 45   | `-i`, `--isolate` | boolean | `isolate = true` |
 46   | `-c`, `--context` | boolean | `context = true` |
 47   
 48   `-c` is the extension's; pi's own `-c` (continue) is intentionally shadowed and unavailable.
 49   Bare `-m` with no following value is a **usage error**.
 50   
 51   ### 3b. Known pi options — a STATIC table; added to `forwardedArgs`
 52   **Value-taking** (consume the next token as the value):
 53   `--provider`, `--model`, `--api-key`, `--system-prompt`, `--append-system-prompt`, `--mode`,
 54   `--name`/`-n`, `--session`, `--session-id`, `--fork`, `--session-dir`, `--tools`/`-t`,
 55   `--exclude-tools`/`-xt`, `--thinking`, `--extension`/`-e`, `--skill`, `--prompt-template`, `--theme`.
 56   
 57   **Boolean** (consume no value):
 58   `--continue`, `--resume`/`-r`, `--no-session`, `--no-tools`/`-nt`, `--no-builtin-tools`/`-nbt`,
 59   `--no-extensions`/`-ne`, `--no-skills`/`-ns`, `--no-prompt-templates`/`-np`, `--no-themes`,
 60   `--no-context-files`/`-nc`, `--verbose`, `--approve`/`-a`, `--no-approve`/`-na`, `--offline`,
 61   `--print`/`-p`.
 62   
 63   Notes:
 64   - This table is a snapshot of `pi --help`; it is maintained by hand. No runtime dependency on
 65     pi's parser for recognition or arity.
 66   - **Reading a value** (applies to every value-taking option, including the extension's `-m`):
 67     the value is the token immediately after the option. If that token **begins with a quote char**
 68     (§6a) and a matching close quote appears later, the value is the text between the quotes —
 69     spanning internal whitespace — with the surrounding quotes **removed**; its content is literal
 70     (no arg parsing, no backslash processing inside — WYSIWYG). Otherwise the value is the next
 71     whitespace-delimited token, verbatim (consumed even if it looks like another option, e.g.
 72     `--thinking --offline` sets thinking's value to `--offline`). There is **no** distinction between
 73     "single-value" and "multi-value" options — every value-taking option reads its value this way, so
 74     `-m gpt56s` ≡ `-m "gpt56s"` and `--system-prompt Psych` ≡ `--system-prompt "Psych"`.
 75     The dequoted value is stored as **one element** in `forwardedArgs`
 76     (e.g. `["--system-prompt", "I am psyched"]`), so pi's `parseArgs` maps it as a single value.
 77     If a value opens with a quote but has no matching close, fall back to the whitespace-delimited token.
 78   - `--print`/`-p` is modeled as **boolean** here (pi's optional-value form would eat prose).
 79   
 80   Value examples:
 81   - `--system-prompt "I am psyched"` → value `I am psyched`.
 82   - `--system-prompt "talk about -m modelname arg"` → value `talk about -m modelname arg` (inner `-m` not parsed).
 83   - `--system-prompt "talk about \-m arg"` → value `talk about \-m arg` (backslash kept; no recursion).
 84   - `-m "gpt56s"` → `modelReference` = `gpt56s`.
 85   
 86   ### 3c. Blocked pi options — rejected
 87   `--models`, `--export`, `--list-models`, `-h`/`--help`, `-v`/`--version`.
 88   Appearing in **args mode** (leading) → hard **error**:
 89   `"/agent does not support <opt>; it would disrupt the background agent run."`
 90   (In prose they are just "known options in the body" → warning, §5.)
 91   
 92   ## 4. Classifying a leading token (args mode), in order
 93   1. **Escaped** (starts with a quote char, or is a backslash-before-dash word) → prose; **flip**. No warning. (§6)
 94   2. **Extension option** (§3a) → consume (+ value for `-m`); stay in args mode.
 95   3. **Blocked pi option** (§3c) → **error**.
 96   4. **Known pi option** (§3b) → consume (+ value if value-taking); push raw token(s) to `forwardedArgs`; stay in args mode.
 97   5. **Anything else** — unknown `--foo` / `-x`, or a non-dash word → **flip to prose**; no warning.
 98   
 99   ## 5. Warnings (prose mode only) — exactly one kind
100   While in prose mode, if an **unescaped, unquoted** token is a **recognized** option
101   (extension §3a, known §3b, or blocked §3c), append this advisory:
102   
103   > ``<opt> [<value>] was included in the prompt body. To specify an argument or an option, place it at the beginning of the command input: /<command> <opt> [<value>] <first-prose-word> …``
104   
105   - `<value>` appears only for value-taking options; it is the token that immediately follows in the input.
106   - `<first-prose-word>` is the first whitespace-delimited word of the prose.
107   - `<command>` is the actual command (`agent` or `agent-isolated`).
108   - Unknown arg-looking tokens in prose (`-g`, `--doesnotexist`) → **no** warning.
109   - Quoted or backslash-escaped option-looking tokens → **no** warning.
110   - Warnings never change the prose text.
111   
112   Worked examples:
113   - `hello world -m gpt56s` → task = whole string; warn `-m gpt56s`, suggest `/agent -m gpt56s hello …`.
114   - `-m gpt56s hello --thinking high world` → `-m gpt56s` parsed; task = `hello --thinking high world`;
115     warn `--thinking high`, suggest `/agent --thinking high hello …`.
116   - `-g badflagname hello world` → `-g` unknown → task = whole string; **no** warning.
117   - `hello world -g badflagname` → task = whole string; **no** warning.
118   - `--doesnotexist this is my message` → `--doesnotexist` unknown → task = whole string; **no** warning.
119   
120   ## 6. Escaping — opt a token out of arg parsing. NEVER recurses.
121   
122   ### 6a. Quotes — kept in prose; stripped ONLY when reading an option value
123   Quote chars: `` ` `` `'` `"` `‘` `’` `“` `”`. Matched pairs: `"…"`, `'…'`, `` `…` ``, `‘…’`, `“…”`.
124   - Inside a matched quote span: no token is treated as an option, and no warning fires.
125   - In **prose**, quotes are **kept verbatim** — they are ordinary characters that merely suppress
126     arg parsing. The one exception is when a quote span is being read as an **option's value**
127     (§3b): there the surrounding quotes are removed and the content becomes the value.
128   - Content inside quotes is literal; a backslash inside quotes is **not** processed (kept).
129   - A quoted span at the very start (not an option value) still flips to prose.
130   - An unmatched quote is just a literal character (no span, no effect).
131   
132   Examples:
133   - `summarize "war and peace"` → task `summarize "war and peace"` (prose → quotes kept).
134   - `"\-m gpt56 hello"` (leading, not a value) → task `"\-m gpt56 hello"` (quotes kept, backslash kept, no arg parsing inside).
135   - `--system-prompt "war and peace"` → value `war and peace` (value → quotes stripped).
136   
137   ### 6b. Backslash-before-dash — the backslash IS removed
138   A backslash at the start of a word whose next char is `-` escapes that word:
139   - Remove the leading `\`; the word (now starting with `-`) is prose. Flip to prose if in args mode;
140     if already in prose, still remove the backslash and emit no warning.
141   - Overly-cautious double form: after removing the leading `\` before `-`, if the next two chars are
142     `\-`, remove that `\` too. So `\-\-word` → `--word`. One backslash also suffices: `\--word` → `--word`.
143   - A backslash **inside quotes** is not processed (see §6a).
144   - A backslash NOT immediately before a `-` is left literal (not an escape).
145   
146   Examples:
147   - `\-m` → `-m`;  `\--thinking` → `--thinking`;  `\-\-thinking` → `--thinking`.
148   - `hello agent, \-m "gpt56s" how are you?` → `hello agent, -m "gpt56s" how are you?`.
149   - `hello agent, \--thi"nking" high` → `hello agent, --thi"nking" high`.
150

152   `forwardedArgs` (known pi options only) is mapped to child-session inputs. Keep the existing
153   mapping to: thinking, model/provider (`resolveCliModel`), tools/excludeTools/noTools, and
154   `resourceLoaderOptions` (system prompt, skills, extensions, prompt-templates, themes, no-* toggles).
155   **Remove** the unknown-flag / `extensionFlagValues` path (there are no unknown flags now) and the
156   `optionConsumesValue` runtime probe (arity now comes from the static table).
157   
158   ## 8. Wiring
159   - `parseAgentCommand` is pure and returns `warnings`.
160   - `startUserAgent` emits each warning via `ctx.ui.notify(warning, "warning")` inside the existing
161     `if (ctx.hasUI)` block. Parse/blocked/usage errors keep flowing through `handleAgentCommand`'s
162     try/catch to `reportCommandError` (unchanged).
163   
164   ## 9. Edge decisions (locked)
165   - Bare `-m` (no value) → usage error.
166   - Empty task after consuming options → usage error.
167   - Blocked option leading → hard error; in prose → warning.
168   - No `--` options terminator (backslash/quotes handle "task starts with a dash").
169   - Value-taking option with no following token → the option is still recorded (no value); no crash.
170   - Multiple known options in prose → one warning per occurrence, in order.

<agent/extensions/pi-user-agents/README.md>
 1   # pi-user-agents
 2   
 3   Your main agent doesn't need to know everything.
 4   
 5   `pi-user-agents` gives the **user** powerful buttons and levers to run, view and control background agents.
 6   
 7   ## Simplest use case
 8   
 9   _Your main agent is in a tool calling frenzy and isn't stopping anytime soon_
10   
11   You:
12   
13       `/agent` plan the next phase and write to phase-2.md.
14   
15   Immediately, this launches a background fork of your main agent while that one is still working on phase 1.
16   
17   When the agent returns, you can view its response.
18   
19   The fork's session can be viewed, steered and aborted in an overlay.
20   
21   ## Commands
22   
23   - `/agent [pi options] [-m MODELNAME] [-i|--isolate] [-c|--context] <task>` gives the child agent the current session context; pass `-i`/`--isolate` to start it without.
24   - `/agent-isolated [pi options] [-m MODELNAME] <task>` is an alias for `/agent -i`.
25   
26   Put options first. The first word that isn't a recognized option ends option parsing; everything from there is your task, kept verbatim (quotes included).
27   
28   ### Passing pi CLI options through
29   
30   Leading `pi` CLI options are forwarded to the child agent as if you had launched `pi` with them — `/agent --thinking high plan the migration`, `/agent --tools read,grep review the diff`, or `/agent --system-prompt "be terse" summarize this`. The recognized set is a curated snapshot of `pi --help` (see `PARSER_SPEC.md` for the full grammar); `-m`/`-i`/`--isolate`/`-c`/`--context` are the extension's own options and are consumed here rather than forwarded.
31   
32   An option typed *after* the task has begun stays in the task and triggers an advisory reminder to move it up front. An unrecognized `-`-token — a typo, or a third-party flag this extension doesn't track — is simply left in the prose, no error. A few options are rejected outright because they would derail a one-shot background run: `--models`, `--export`, `--list-models`, `-h`/`--help`, `-v`/`--version`.
33   
34   To keep an option-looking word in the task, quote it (`summarize "-m stays literal"`) or backslash-escape it (`explain \--thinking`) — quotes stay in the prompt, the leading backslash is removed. An option's value may be quoted to include spaces: `--system-prompt "be terse and precise"`.
35   
36   By default the entire run is invisible to the main agent, forever: the invocation, the child's tool calling, and the result never enter its context. The result renders in the transcript as a TUI-only session entry (persisted, survives reloads) — for your eyes only. With `-c`/`--context`, the run is still invisible while in flight, but on completion the result — carrying your verbatim command invocation in a `<user_invocation>` tag — is delivered to the main agent ASAP, like a steering message: steered into its current turn if one is streaming, or triggering an immediate response if it is idle.
37   
38   The widget below the editor shows active and recently completed agents. Use `←` or `↓` to select it, `Enter` to open an agent overlay, and `x` to stop a running agent or dismiss a completed one.
39   
40   ### Context window meter
41   
42   Each agent row places a one-cell context meter between the command and its prompt:
43   
44   ```text
45   ✓ User agents
46     ↑↓ select · Enter view · x dispose · Esc back
47   └─ ⏺ ✓ /agent ▇ i am testing the widget now - read a ton...
48        ⎿  Loaded several large Pi source and documentation...
49   ```
50   
51   The meter shows how much of that child agent's selected model context window is in use. It has eight 12.5% bins—`▁▂▃▄▅▆▇█`—and shifts from white toward red as the context fills. Completed rows retain their final reading. The extension reads Pi's resolved model and live session context usage, so model-specific limits and configured `contextWindow` overrides are respected; when Pi cannot provide a usage percentage, the meter is omitted rather than guessed.
52   
53   The overlay shows the agent's full rolling conversation — user prompts, assistant turns, tool calls, and tool results — and follows the tail while the agent streams. Scroll up to pause following; `End` resumes it.
54   
55   ## Steering a live agent
56   
57   While an agent is still running, press `Enter` in its overlay to open the **Steer** input. Submit a message with `Enter`; Pi queues it after the agent's current turn and tool work, before its next model call. `Esc` cancels the composer.
58   
59   Steering is available only while the child session is active. After the agent has produced its final response, the extension disposes that session; the overlay remains available to read the captured transcript or copy the result, but it is no longer interactive.
60   
61   ## Result delivery — Pi SDK mental model
62   
63   How a finished run reaches (or hides from) the main agent rests on two Pi SDK channels with very different context semantics:
64   
65   - **`pi.sendMessage(message, { deliverAs, triggerTurn })`** — custom messages ALWAYS reach the main agent's LLM context eventually. The options form a first-match-wins chain (see `sendCustomMessage` in pi's `dist/core/agent-session.js`):
66     1. `deliverAs: "nextTurn"` → buffered in memory, spliced in alongside the user's next prompt; `triggerTurn` ignored; not persisted — lost if the session ends first. Still reaches the agent eventually.
67     2. Agent streaming → `"followUp"` queues for after the run finishes; `"steer"` (default) injects after the current tool batch, before the next LLM call. `triggerTurn` ignored. Queues drain before `agent_end` — messages are never dropped.
68     3. Agent idle + `triggerTurn: true` → appended and an LLM turn starts immediately.
69     4. Agent idle otherwise → silently appended to context; the agent sees it on whatever turn comes next.
70   
71     In short: `deliverAs` only matters while streaming; `triggerTurn` only matters while idle.
72   
73   - **`pi.appendEntry(customType, data)` + `pi.registerEntryRenderer`** — the only channel that renders in the transcript while staying out of LLM context *forever*. Entries are persisted in the session file and re-rendered on reload. The entry's `data` is optional in the type — renderers must guard it.
74   
75   This extension maps the two extremes onto the `-c` flag: the default posts the result card via `appendEntry` (main agent structurally oblivious), and `-c` posts a custom message with `{ triggerTurn: true }` (steered mid-turn or answered immediately). Both channels share one card renderer in `transcript.ts`.
76   
77   ---
78   
79   Heavily inspired by [tintinweb/pi-subagents](https://github.com/tintinweb/pi-subagents).
80

336   	const commandMatch = /^\/(agent-isolated|agent)(?=$|\s)/.exec(line);
337   	if (!commandMatch || cursor <= commandMatch[0].length || cursor > line.length) return undefined;
338   	const command = commandMatch[1] as AgentCommandName;

340   	const expectation = analyzeArgumentCursor(line.slice(argumentOffset), cursor - argumentOffset, command);
341   	if (!expectation) return undefined;

349   function analyzeArgumentCursor(args: string, cursor: number, command: AgentCommandName): AgentCursorExpectation | undefined {
350   	const usedSemanticIds = new Set<string>(command === "agent-isolated" ? ["isolate"] : []);
351   	let position = 0;
352   	let expectedValueOption: AgentOptionDefinition | undefined;
353   
354   	for (;;) {
355   		while (position < args.length && /\s/.test(args[position] ?? "")) position += 1;
356   		if (position >= cursor) {
357   			if (expectedValueOption) {
358   				return valueExpectation(command, "", cursor, cursor, expectedValueOption, false, usedSemanticIds);
359   			}
360   			return optionExpectation(command, "", cursor, cursor, usedSemanticIds);
361   		}
362   
363   		if (expectedValueOption) {
364   			const value = readCursorValue(args, position);
365   			if (cursor <= value.end) {
366   				const fragmentStart = value.quoted ? value.start + 1 : value.start;
367   				const fragmentEnd = value.quoted ? Math.max(fragmentStart, value.end - 1) : value.end;
368   				return valueExpectation(
369   					command,
370   					args.slice(fragmentStart, cursor),
371   					fragmentStart,
372   					fragmentEnd,
373   					expectedValueOption,
374   					value.quoted,
375   					usedSemanticIds,
376   				);
377   			}
378   			position = value.end;
379   			expectedValueOption = undefined;
380   			continue;
381   		}
382   
383   		const tokenStart = position;
384   		while (position < args.length && !/\s/.test(args[position] ?? "")) position += 1;
385   		const tokenEnd = position;
386   		if (cursor <= tokenEnd) {
387   			const fragment = args.slice(tokenStart, cursor);
388   			if (!fragment.startsWith("-")) return undefined;
389   			return optionExpectation(command, fragment, tokenStart, tokenEnd, usedSemanticIds);
390   		}
391   
392   		const token = args.slice(tokenStart, tokenEnd);
393   		const option = OPTION_BY_NAME.get(token);
394   		if (!option || option.role === "blocked") return undefined;
395   		usedSemanticIds.add(option.semanticId);
396   		if (option.arity === "value") expectedValueOption = option;
397   	}

448   		const closer = QUOTE_PAIRS[text[index] ?? ""];
449   		const close = closer === undefined ? -1 : text.indexOf(closer, index + 1);
450   		if (close === -1) {

452   			continue;
453   		}

460   function collectProseWarnings(prose: string, quoteMask: boolean[], command: AgentCommandName): string[] {
461   	const tokens: { text: string; index: number }[] = [];
462   	const pattern = /\S+/g;
463   	for (let match = pattern.exec(prose); match !== null; match = pattern.exec(prose)) {
464   		tokens.push({ text: match[0], index: match.index });
465   	}
466   	const firstToken = tokens[0];
467   	const firstProseWord = quoteMask[firstToken.index] ? firstToken.text : unescapeWord(firstToken.text);
468   	const warnings: string[] = [];
469   	for (let index = 0; index < tokens.length; index += 1) {
470   		const token = tokens[index];
471   		if (quoteMask[token.index]) continue;
472   		const option = OPTION_BY_NAME.get(token.text);
473   		if (!option) continue;
474   		const value = option.arity === "value" ? tokens[index + 1]?.text : undefined;
475   		const optionWithValue = value === undefined ? token.text : `${token.text} ${value}`;
476   		warnings.push(
477   			`${optionWithValue} was included in the prompt body. To specify an argument or an option, place it at the beginning of the command input: /${command} ${optionWithValue} ${firstProseWord} …`,
478   		);
479   	}
480   	return warnings;

483   function unescapeWord(word: string): string {
484   	if (!word.startsWith("\\-")) return word;
485   	const unescaped = word.slice(1);
486   	return unescaped.startsWith("-\\-") ? `-${unescaped.slice(2)}` : unescaped;

293   function subscribeToChildSession(session: AgentSession, runningAgent: RunningAgent, widget: UserAgentWidget): () => void {

297   		if (event.type === "agent_settled") logSteering(runningAgent.id, "child-agent-settled", { streaming: session.isStreaming });
298   		if (event.type === "turn_start") logSteering(runningAgent.id, "turn-started", { streaming: session.isStreaming });
299   		if (event.type === "turn_end") logSteering(runningAgent.id, "turn-ended", { streaming: session.isStreaming });
300   		if (event.type === "message_start") logSteering(runningAgent.id, "message-started", { role: event.message.role, streaming: session.isStreaming });
301   		const finalizedMessageUpdate = event.type === "message_update" && event.assistantMessageEvent.type.endsWith("_end");
302   		if (finalizedMessageUpdate || event.type === "message_end") runningAgent.latestFinalizedMessage = structuredClone(event.message);
303   		if (finalizedMessageUpdate && event.message.role === "assistant" && event.assistantMessageEvent.type === "text_end") {
304   			runningAgent.responseText = assistantText(event.message);
305   		}
306   		if (event.type === "message_end" && event.message.role === "assistant") runningAgent.responseText = assistantText(event.message);
307   		if (event.type === "tool_execution_start") {
308   			runningAgent.activeTools.set(event.toolCallId, event.toolName);
309   		}
310   		if (event.type === "tool_execution_end") {
311   			runningAgent.activeTools.delete(event.toolCallId);
312   			runningAgent.toolUses += 1;
313   		}
314   		if (event.type === "turn_end") {
315   			runningAgent.turnCount += 1;
316   		}
317   		if (event.type === "message_update" && !finalizedMessageUpdate) return;
318   		widget.update();
319   	});
320   }

322   function assistantText(message: Extract<AgentMessage, { role: "assistant" }>): string {
323   	return message.content
324   		.filter((part) => part.type === "text")
325   		.map((part) => part.text)
326   		.join("\n");

329   function getFinalAssistantText(session: AgentSession): string {
330   	const assistantMessages = session.agent.state.messages.filter((message) => message.role === "assistant");
331   	const lastMessage = assistantMessages.at(-1);
332   	if (!lastMessage) throw new Error("User agent finished without an assistant message");
333   	if (lastMessage.stopReason === "error" || lastMessage.stopReason === "aborted") {
334   		throw new Error(lastMessage.errorMessage ?? `User agent ${lastMessage.stopReason}`);

338   	if (!text) throw new Error("User agent returned no text response");
